sn56.41:1.3: “Speculation about the world” is said to be one of the four trains of thought that can drive you mad (AN 4.77:1.9). At MN 48:8.9 it is distinguished as speculation about this world and the next. | The Buddha once visited the Sumāgadhā pond to accept Nigrodha’s challenge. There was a peacock’s feeding ground nearby. The Rāmāyaṇa describes the river Sumāgadhī, which rises among the five hills of Rajagaha like a gorgeous garland (1.31.7); this must be a lake on that river. Perhaps to be identified with the modern Dhadhar.
sn56.41:3.4: The titans and the gods are normally depicted as human-sized. The commentaries say they employed the Sambaru sorcery to escape the gods (SN 11.23:1.8).
sn56.41:4.1: The sequence of ideas is not really coherent: the Buddha has said that such speculation will drive you mad; then that the man was in fact not mad; then says this is a reason to not do it (the parallel at SA 407 is similar). It’s also unclear what his speculations had to do with the titans entering the lotus stalk: he just happened to be there when it happened. If, however, in his contemplations he fell into samādhi and had a truthful psychic vision, what exactly is the problem? The only issue, as far as the Sutta says, is not the speculation itself, but that oneself and others will think that you’re mad.
